newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Kiwi Air founder vows to fight six fraud charges.
newsitem.headline: Kiwi Air founder vows to fight six fraud charges.

text.p: Kiwi Airline founder Ewan Wilson repeated his vow to fight six fraud charges against him "all the way" after a brief appearance in Hamilton District Court on Monday, the New Zealand Press Association reported.

The 30-year-old former Kiwi chief executive arrived at the courthouse and was shepherded up the stairs by his lawyer David Wilson, wife Monique Blain, and a support group of former Kiwi staff wearing Kiwi Air t-shirts.
A large turnout of journalists and photographers surrounded him as he entered the court and later as he held an impromptu news conference on the courthouse steps.
Wilson faces five counts that on or about June 23, 1995, he used a document for pecuniary advantage or benefit to himself or another.

He is also charged with making a statement on June 29, 1995, before his then-lawyer David Nielsen confirming he paid for his newly issued shares in Kiwi out of his own resources and that the money did not come from overseas or any foreign airline, foreign company or foreign country.

The charge goes on to say Wilson also stated the increased share capital was made up from shareholders' cash resources of $500,000 and capitalised profit of $258,000. The police charge says the statement would amount to perjury if it was made on oath in a judicial proceeding.
Wilson's appearance, before registrar Mike Douglas, lasted for less than 10 minutes.
Wilson, whose airline collapsed on September 9, was remanded on a bail bond to reappear on April 3 for the taking of depositions on the charges to see if there is a case to answer.
Police insisted as a condition of bail that Wilson be ordered by Douglas to surrender his passport. Wilson told the court he had a British and a New Zealand passport.
David Wilson told the court his client elected trial by jury and would defend all charges against him.
There was no application for name suppression.
Wilson said after hearing the charges against him for the first time today he was very comfortable with his stance to "fight these allegations all the way".
A tearful Blain, who was a director of the failed airline and a staff member, said it was "terrible to be so discredited for supplying a new service".

Kiwi, which grew out of Wilson's city travel agency and charter operation into an international timetabled carrier, sparked a trans-Tasman fare war in 1995, offering no frills "nuts and cola" seat prices to Brisbane and Sydney from Hamilton and Dunedin.

Liquidators Price Waterhouse of Auckland say the full extent of Kiwi's losses and creditors may never be known, but it is thought Kiwi had debts of up to $7 million, some of it to pre-paid passengers.
